newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher, Jan PPI bolsters market.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher, Jan PPI bolsters market.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher in moderate trade as a friendly wholesale inflation report bolstered the market and encouraged investors to set some long positions ahead of the weekend, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 17/32 at 101-8/32, yielding 6.53 percent.

The market closed early on Friday at 1400 EST/1900 GMT following a recommendation by the PSA The Bond Market Trade Association. The market will remain closed Monday for the observance of the President's Day holiday.
Trading in New York will resume at normal hours on Tuesday, February 18.
Players turned bullish after the Labor Department released a lower-than-expected Producer Price Index report for Janaury.
The overall index was down 0.3 percent, the first drop since October 1994. The core index, which excludes energy and food price variations, was unchanged.

"Inflation continues to come on the low side ... I think (PPI) came below what anybody had even dreamed of coming up with for the total," said Astrid Adolfson, economist at consulting firm MCM MoneyWatch Inc.

Market players also learned that January industrial output was unchanged against a revised 0.5 percent rise in December. January capacity utilization was at 83.3 percent against 83.5 percent the previous month.

A coupon pass by the Federal Reserve by mid-morning also provided some underpinning. The Fed added permanent reserves to the system by buying coupons with maturity dates ranging from August 31, 1997 to August 15, 1998.
The Fed bought securities for delivery on Tuesday.
Analysts said the Fed is now expected to return to the market with extra rounds of coupon passes next week.

"We expect the Fed to come in next week with more coupon passes and finish the job," a trader at a U.S. investment bank said, referring to the fact that the central bank usually buys bills and then notes and bonds.
Analysts said the yield curve is expected to flatten a bit as the short-end of the spectrum becomes a little expensive for the current economic outlook.
"Unless you believe the Fed's next move will be an easing (of monetary policy), it's hard to get much further movement at the short end," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

"The short-end is against the wall and therefore anything you are likely to see will probably be in the intermediate to the long end of the curve and that's approaching an overbought condition," Liro added.
The spead between the long bond and the two-year note yields ended Friday's session at 76 basis points against the 87-point gap posted on February 5.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down three basis points at 4.96 percent. The six-month bill rate fell three points to 4.96 percent. The year bill rate was down three points at 5.15 percent.

The two-year note closed up 2/32 at 100-6/32, yielding 5.77 percent. The five-year note traded up 5/32 at 100-25/32 to yield 6.06 percent. The ten-year note closed up 10/32 at 99-28/32, yielding 6.27 percent.
